items.questionEn: Have you ever encountered a lightning strike during flight?
items.answerEn: No, I have never encountered a lightning strike during flight. I know that lightning strikes are dangerous, so I avoid them during flight.
items.riskAssessment: First-person content is an adjustable practice answer and contains no experience beyond the selected variant.

items.questionEn: What should a pilot do if the aircraft is struck by lightning during flight?
editActions: selected the most complete legacy variant
items.answerEn: I would first maintain control of the aircraft and follow the SOP and checklist. I would check for structural or system damage and report the situation to ATC. If the damage were severe, I would request a diversion to an alternate airport. After landing, I would request a maintenance inspection.
items.riskAssessment: All actions come from the selected v1 variant; no checklist action or limit was added.

items.questionEn: What measures can pilots take to reduce the risk of a lightning strike?
items.answerEn: Before flight, I check the weather reports and avoid areas where lightning is likely. During flight, I monitor the weather radar and request a deviation from ATC if lightning is detected ahead. I also avoid cumulonimbus clouds and thunderstorm areas.
items.riskAssessment: The answer retains only weather review, radar monitoring, deviation, and thunderstorm avoidance from v1.

items.questionEn: Why must an aircraft take off within the applicable holdover time after ground de-icing or anti-icing?
items.answerEn: Anti-icing fluid loses effectiveness over time. If takeoff is delayed beyond the applicable holdover time, ice, snow, or frost may accumulate again on critical surfaces. This contamination can reduce lift and increase drag, so the aircraft must be treated again before takeoff.
items.riskAssessment: The variable numerical range was excluded; every retained consequence and action is present in v1.

items.questionEn: What should pilots do if they hear a "GO-AROUND, WINDSHEAR AHEAD" warning during approach?
items.answerEn: The pilots should go around immediately. They should use TOGA thrust, maintain the required configuration until clear of the wind shear, and closely monitor airspeed, altitude, attitude, and vertical speed.
items.riskAssessment: The fixed 15-degree pitch value and conflicting configuration changes were excluded rather than supplemented.

items.questionEn: How many evacuation slides are installed on the aircraft type you fly?
items.answerEn: I fly the C172, which has no evacuation slides.
items.riskAssessment: The aircraft type and zero-slide answer are both stated in the selected v1 variant.

items.questionEn: Have you ever encountered an emergency, urgency, or distress situation during a flight? If so, what happened?
items.answerEn: No, I have never encountered an emergency, urgency, or distress situation during a flight. However, I have practised responses to engine failure, depressurization, and turbulence in simulator training, using SOPs and checklists.
items.riskAssessment: No real event is invented; the simulator experience is explicit in v1.

items.questionEn: What general steps should a pilot take in an urgency or distress situation?
items.answerEn: I would keep control of the aircraft and ask the copilot to read the checklist while I carry out the required actions. At the same time, I would report the situation to ATC. If necessary, I would request a diversion, priority landing, and emergency services.
items.riskAssessment: The answer stays at the general level of the source and adds no emergency-specific checklist steps.

items.questionEn: What do you learn during dangerous goods training?
items.answerEn: During dangerous goods training, we learn the regulations and categories of dangerous goods. We also learn how to identify and check them, how they should be transported, and how to deal with a leak during flight.
items.riskAssessment: Every training topic is present in the two selected v1 segments.

items.questionEn: What is a cockpit voice recorder (CVR)?
items.answerEn: CVR stands for Cockpit Voice Recorder. It records cockpit audio, including crew communications, radio transmissions, warnings, and background sounds. The recordings can provide important information for accident investigations.
items.riskAssessment: The time-duration value was excluded; no replacement value was added.

items.questionEn: What is your opinion on using CVR recordings to monitor flight crews?
items.answerEn: I think using CVR recordings for supervision can be useful. It can encourage crews to follow SOPs, maintain professional communication, and reduce irrelevant talk in the cockpit. These practices can improve flight safety.
items.riskAssessment: The answer expresses only the positive supervisory rationale contained in v1 and does not invent a company policy.

items.questionEn: What is a Minimum Equipment List (MEL)?
items.answerEn: MEL stands for Minimum Equipment List. It is an important document for aircraft dispatch because it tells the crew whether a flight can be conducted when equipment is inoperative.

items.questionEn: What communication practices should pilots use when speaking with ATC?
items.answerEn: Pilots should use standard phraseology, speak clearly, and read back instructions correctly. If a clearance is unclear, they should confirm it with ATC. They should stay focused and avoid distractions so that information is transmitted accurately.
items.riskAssessment: All communication practices are explicitly listed in the selected v1 segment.

I would mediate impartially and remind them that teamwork and professional communication are essential to flight safety. I would then help them resolve the misunderstanding so they could focus on their duties and the flight.

items.questionEn: What factors can cause a tail strike?
editActions: excluded an unauthorized v2 image-source mapping
items.answerEn: A tail strike can result from improper control, such as an excessive rotation rate, an early flare, or over-rotation during a go-around. Other factors include an unstable approach, incorrect stabilizer trim, poor crosswind handling, a centre-of-gravity calculation error, strong wind shear, or wake turbulence.
